0.headline: Passenger mobility company Chartered Speed cuts IPO size to Rs 433 crore after SEBI regulatory changes
0.heading: Passenger mobility company Chartered Speed cuts IPO size to Rs 433 crore after SEBI regulatory changes
0.intro: Chartered Speed IPO | The revised public issue will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 333 crore and an offer-for-sale of Rs 100 crore.
0.body:
Ahmedabad-headquartered passenger mobility company Chartered Speed has reduced the size of its proposed initial public offering (IPO) to Rs 433 crore, following changes in the regulatory framework introduced by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).

The revised IPO will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 333 crore and an offer-for-sale (OFS) of Rs 100 crore.

Under the OFS, promoters Pankaj Gandhi and his wife, Alka Gandhi, will each sell shares worth up to Rs 50 crore.

Through its regulations dated April 13 and a communication to the Association of Investment Bankers dated October 12 this year, SEBI allowed companies to increase or decrease the size of their fresh issue by up to 50 percent without refiling their draft red herring prospectus (DRHP). Chartered Speed has accordingly reduced the size of its fresh issue.

Click Here To Read All IPO News

The company had filed its draft IPO papers with the capital markets regulator in September 2025, seeking to raise Rs 855 crore. The proposed IPO comprised a fresh issue of Rs 655 crore and an OFS of Rs 200 crore. SEBI subsequently approved the company's IPO papers in January 2026.

The company has also revised the proposed utilisation of the fresh issue proceeds. Of the net proceeds, Rs 50.2 crore will be used to purchase electric buses, while Rs 205 crore will go towards debt repayment. The remaining amount will be utilised for general corporate purposes.

At the time of filing its DRHP in September 2025, Chartered Speed had an operational fleet of more than 2,000 buses as of June 2025, including 46 electric buses.

In its draft papers, the company stated that it intended to gradually phase out vehicles powered by fossil fuels, with a strong focus on sustainability. It had also set a target of converting 25 percent of its fleet into electric vehicles.

Motilal Oswal Investment Advisors and SBI Capital Markets have been appointed as the merchant bankers to manage the Chartered Speed IPO.

1.headline: Pristine Logistics, Arohan Financial Services get SEBI nod to launch IPOs
1.heading: Pristine Logistics, Arohan Financial Services get SEBI nod to launch IPOs
1.intro: Arohan Financial Services approached the capital markets regulator by filing its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) in May 2026, while Pristine Logistics & Infraprojects submitted its draft offer document through the confidential filing route in June.
1.body:
Pristine Logistics &amp; Infraprojects and Arohan Financial Services have received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to proceed with their initial public offerings (IPOs) and raise funds from the primary market.

Arohan Financial Services, a microfinance institution, approached the capital markets regulator by filing its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) in May 2026, while Pristine Logistics &amp; Infraprojects submitted its draft offer document through the confidential filing route in June.

SEBI issued its observations on Arohan Financial Services' draft offer document on November 13 and on Pristine Logistics' filing on November 19, allowing the companies to proceed with their IPO plans within the stipulated timelines of 12 months and 18 months, respectively.

Under the regular filing route, a company has 12 months from the date of receiving SEBI's observations to launch its IPO. In the case of confidential filings, the company gets an 18-month window to proceed with the offering. However, it must first submit an updated DRHP to SEBI, followed by filing the red herring prospectus with the Registrar of Companies (RoC), before opening the IPO, subject to the applicable regulatory requirements.

Arohan Financial Services, a technology-enabled non-banking financial company (NBFC) operating in the microfinance segment, plans to raise Rs 600 crore through a fresh issue, which includes a proposed pre-IPO placement of Rs 120 crore. Additionally, existing investors will offload 4.04 crore equity shares through an offer-for-sale (OFS).

Teachers Insurance and Annuity Association of America, Aavishkaar Goodwell India Microfinance Development Company, Tano India Private Equity Fund, Maj Invest Financial Inclusion Fund, Danish Sustainable Development Goals Investment Fund, and Michael &amp; Susan Dell Foundation will be among the shareholders selling their stakes through the OFS.

Click Here To Read All IPO News

The NBFC proposes to utilise the net proceeds from the fresh issue to augment its capital base to meet future business requirements, including onward lending, and for general corporate purposes.

Meanwhile, Pristine Logistics &amp; Infraprojects operates a rail-focused multimodal logistics platform, providing integrated logistics infrastructure and services for both containerised and non-containerised cargo.

The company is promoted by Amit Kumar, Durgesh Govil, Rajnish Kumar and Sanjay Mawar, who bring experience across Indian Railways, Container Corporation of India (CONCOR), rail infrastructure development, logistics and legal services.

Pristine offers a range of services, including EXIM and domestic container logistics, rail transportation, rail bulk transportation, warehousing, container maintenance and repair, and mining logistics following its acquisition of Sical Logistics.

Apart from these two companies, SEBI has also cleared theIPO offer documents of Advanced Sys-Tek and Assetz during the week.

2.headline: OPINION | Anthropic’s IPO and the changing ways retail investors participate in the AI market
2.heading: OPINION | Anthropic’s IPO and the changing ways retail investors participate in the AI market
2.intro: The IPO was a trendsetter and expanded retail opportunities to participate in the AI boom. Through ETFs and tokenised products, however, a wider cohort of retail investors across the world has jumped in. But risks need careful monitoring
2.body:
For much of the AI boom, only a relatively small group of investors had access to the biggest investment opportunities. Early funding rounds in companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic were largely reserved for venture capital firms, institutional investors, and wealthy individuals. By the time these companies became accessible to the wider market, much of their early growth had already taken place. 

Anthropic’s IPO expands the retail pathway

Anthropic’s IPO marks an important shift in this landscape. It is not just another technology company entering the public markets. It reflects how the opportunity to invest in artificial intelligence is gradually moving beyond private investment circles and becoming accessible to a wider set of investors. 

However, the way retail investors participate in this opportunity is changing. An IPO is only one route. Investors are increasingly finding exposure through public markets, investment funds, and products that hold stakes in private companies. 

The IPO is changing the access conversation 

One of the most important aspects of Anthropic’s public offering is the scale of capital being raised. This means the IPO is not simply an exit for early investors. A significant part of the capital raised is intended to support the company's next phase of growth. 

Retail participation has also become an important part of the IPO process, with a portion of the offering made available through brokerage platforms. But access does not necessarily mean equal opportunity. Retail allocations are limited, demand can exceed supply, and investors buying after listing may have to pay a market price significantly different from the IPO price. 

Institutional and early-stage investors have participated in the company's growth over several years. Retail investors entering at the IPO stage are evaluating the business at a much later point in its journey, when expectations around growth and valuation are already reflected in the price. 

Retail access is expanding beyond IPOs 

Retail investors are finding ways to participate in the AI boom without having to pick individual winners or wait for an IPO. AI-themed ETFs have grown rapidly, with assets reportedly rising from $10.3 billion to $64.9 billion in a year. Investors are also gaining exposure through semiconductor funds, broad market index funds and mutual funds that already hold stakes in private AI companies such as Anthropic. 

Some are seeking earlier exposure through private-market funds and tokenised or derivative products, while leveraged ETFs and options offer ways to take larger positions with less upfront capital. However, these routes come with different risks, including high fees, limited liquidity, leverage and, in some cases, no direct ownership in the underlying company. 

Access to AI investments is expanding, but it does not necessarily mean better diversification or lower risk. As investors look beyond IPOs, understanding what they actually own, how much they pay for access, and how easily they can exit becomes just as important as choosing the investment itself. 

What this means for Indian investors 

For Indian retail investors, access to global AI opportunities is also evolving. While the Anthropic IPO prospectus does not constitute an offer to the public in India, investors may explore overseas investment routes after listing, subject to applicable regulations and eligibility requirements. 

These include investing through the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), eligible GIFT City platforms, tokenized stocks, and Indian mutual funds with international exposure. Each route has different costs, investment limits, tax implications, and operational requirements. Investors should understand these before making a decision. 

The larger opportunity for Indian investors is that participation in the AI economy no longer has to depend on identifying one company at the right time. Exposure can come from across the value chain, including software, chips, cloud infrastructure, and other businesses supporting AI adoption. 

The next phase of AI investing 

Anthropic's IPO is part of a broader change in how investment opportunities are reaching retail investors. The boundary between private and public markets is becoming less rigid, and financial products are creating new ways to access businesses at different stages of growth. 

But wider access should not be confused with lower risk. Investors must evaluate the underlying business, understand the structure of the product, account for fees and liquidity, and ensure that the investment fits their financial goals.  

The real opportunity is not simply to get access to the next big AI company. It is to understand where value is being created across the AI ecosystem and participate in that growth through informed, well-planned investment decisions. 

&nbsp;

(Prateek Gupta, Head of Business, Mudrex.) 

Views are personal and do not represent the stand of this publication.
